title: Leading AI Change — The Human Side of Responsible Deployment

segments.text: Good morning everyone and thank you for
being here. Um as mentioned my name is
Dana Sasa and I lead people change
management for advanced analytics and AI
here at CIBC. Um and for the next 20
minutes or so I'm going to talk about a
topic that I think doesn't get as much
attention during AI transformations. Um
but in my opinion is equally important
to the technical aspects of things as
well. And the reason I say that is
because you can build the platform, you
can launch the tool, you can put all the
technical pieces in place, but if your
people don't understand it, they don't
understand how to embed it in their ways
of working and they don't trust it. You
the value of that tool is never going to
fully materialize. And so today I'm
going to walk you through a case study
based on some work we've done from a
change management perspective here at
CIBC. what we solved for, what the
results look like, and also share some
lessons that surfaced from that
experience as well that hopefully can
inspire you as you embark on AI
initiatives as well.
All right, so I think I'll just ground
us with a common scenario that I think
many of us have faced. Um, an
organization heavily invests in AI. Uh,
the technology is built, the platform is
launched, you know, communications go
out, town halls are held. Um, and six
months later, the technology is working
exactly as expected, but adoption is
much lower than anticipated. And it's
not usually because the tool itself is
not helpful. And it's also not because
people are unwilling to adapt. It's
really because the human side was never
addressed with the same level of
intention as the technology. And that
can show up in many different ways.
Managers don't understand how to talk
about AI with their teams. uh team
members uh lack confidence in the tool
and and fear what it means for their
jobs. And then you also have leaders
who, you know, supported the investment
of the tool but are not actually making
the connection points to how it actually
fits into day-to-day work. And that
really is where you're going to see some
of that anxiety and uncertainty sort of
level up in that space. And that's
really where that people change strategy
is going to be an imperative part of
your uh strategy there.
And so what I'll walk through today is
how you can sort of design a tailored
change strategy to support the
technology adoption as well.
Um but before I sort of jump right into
that, I want to take a minute to just
talk about why AI adoption is uniquely
hard. We can talk about it being
emotional, fastmoving, role dependent.
Um and naturally there's a lot of
uncertainty and anxiety with this as
well. people are naturally going to ask
questions about what does this mean for
my job? Um, you know, how what does this
change for my expectations? Um, and
those questions don't necessarily
surface directly. It's going to surface
in the sense of quiet resistance and
hesitation, apprehension in the tools.
You'll also see that trust is quite
uneven. you're going to have one side
which is very excited about AI, eager to
jump into things and maybe is a little
overly reliant on the tool or perhaps
isn't necess aren't necessarily putting
in the right checkpoints to validate the
outputs. But on the other side, you have
a huge population who doesn't even want
to touch the tool out of fear for what
this means for their job and also from a
lack of confidence in trying to use
something like that. Fundamentally, I
think we all know it's going to change
how we do our work. And this is not just
a typical tech transformation, right? It
naturally, as I said, introduces anxiety
and some lack of confidence. And so, you
have to approach your change management
approach from the lens of thinking about
going a little bit deeper. This is a
behavioral change. You are fundamentally
changing the ways that people are uh
completing their daily tasks and that
needs to be taken into consideration.
and four and five year it feels complex
and the landscape moves fast. All of
these acronyms, terminology, concepts,
they can feel very overwhelming for
someone who is not familiar with the
space and it feels like they need to
become an expert overnight. And with a
space like AI where use cases are
popping up every single day, um it can
feel very overwhelming to try to keep up
with that. And of course, one of the
biggest challenges is relevance.
Relevance is role dependent. what is
important to a project manager is not
going to be important to a frontline
employee or an executive leader. And so
unless you can actually effectively
communicate how that AI is going to fit
into their day-to-day work, you're going
to see that the adoption is going to
stall more at an experimental phase
rather than actually being embedded into
ways of working. And so with the uh case
study that I'm going to walk through,
all of these challenges showed up and
really helped to inform the approach
that we decided to take.
And so in terms of what we set out to
do, this was actually one of CIBC's most
um significant AI transformations. And
this was the enterprisewide rollout of
our generative AI tool, KAI. And this
was rolled out to over 50,000 employees
across the organization across every
line of business. And so, as I said, a
major step in the bank's AI journey. But
as you can imagine, in a high highly
regulated risk sensitive environment
like ours, the objective is not simply
to make the tool available. The
objective is to ensure that people
understand what the tool is, how to
safely use it, and then actually start
to think about how they integrate that
into their ways of working. And so when
we think about that, you know, we we
knew given how significant this was to
AI, the AI journey at CIBC, our change
management approach needed to be
structured in a very similar way. And so
our intention was to ensure and it was
very deliberate that our change strategy
was intentional, fully supported and
structured in a way that was very
similar to how our technical side of
things was also supported as well.
And so before I show you the results
from that, I'll go into maybe
establishing a similar shared vocabulary
here. Um and I think you know this is
important because a lot of AI
initiatives tend to stall uh because
organizations are measuring the wrong
thing. There is an important distinction
between deployment and adoption. They
are not the same thing. And I think the
way to think about it is through four
stages. So you start with access. You
know folks have access to the tool. It
exists. They can log in. The second
piece is on usage. So people open it
occasionally. they can experiment with
it. It's a little bit more ad hoc. Then
you go into adoption. This is really
where you're going to see that
behavioral change start to come to life.
People are embedding the tool into their
ways of working. And then building on
that, you go into fluency. So, not only
are they using the tool and embedding it
in their ways of working, but they're
actually actively advocating for it.
they're sharing best practices with
their teams um to ensure that all their
colleagues are coming along on this
journey as well and it fundamentally is
becoming part of the organizational
culture as it is embedded in their daily
workflows. And so this is really the I
want to say metrics or the measurement
lens that we took as we look to assess
the success of our rollout. And I would
argue that a lot of AI initiatives
across organizations, we take a look at
access and usage and then we say, you
know what, we see light usage and the
tool is available. We call it a success.
But where you're really going to see the
value come to life is in adoption and
then really visibly see it when it
reaches fluency. That's when that
behavioral change starts to shift.
Um and so keeping those four sort of
stages in mind I think it makes it uh
much clearer to understand what a
structured change management approach
can make possible. Um so as you can see
we onboarded over 50,000 users across
the bank. So if you think about that
first stage in access cannot check check
that off and say we've done that at
scale. Um, but then if we move forward,
we're actually seeing over 25,000
individuals who are daily active users
of the tool. What this tells us is that
not only are we seeing that it's being
embedded into their daily workflows, but
we're seeing that behavioral change and
it's continuing to trend upward. And
further to that, we can also assess from
a metrics perspective that we're seeing
over 6,000 users at CIBC just over the
course of a year who have reached expert
level fluency in leveraging the tool.
And that's 100% increase year-to- date
growth and which tells us that
capability uh building is not just
deepening um but it's also broadening as
well. And beyond that, we also are
seeing not only are they experts with
using the tool, but they're sharing that
knowledge as well. We have an internal
AI marketplace um where folks have built
agents and they publish those for others
to be able to leverage as well. So they
share that with their team members. And
what we're seeing from that in terms of
subscription levels to over thousands of
agents or reuse or inspiration from that
is really fundamentally changing the way
our employees are working. And so when
you start to see that your employees are
not just using the tool, but they are
using it to build their own platforms,
share that with other people. you're not
just seeing, you know, tool usage
anymore. You're actually seeing an
organizational culture shift. And so
with that sort of in mind, I want to say
that doesn't just happen by itself. Of
course, you need to have a structured
change management approach to support
that. You need to have the constructs in
place to support your people throughout
this journey and ensure that they, you
know, understand how they can leverage
these tools and and potentially move
themselves through this fluency as well.
Um, and so sort of building on that,
I'll just talk a little bit about
building the conditions for adoption. So
I want to say there wasn't necessarily
one specific lever that contributed to
the success of this roll out, but rather
it was eight different levers working
together in a little bit of a system.
The first one being executive
sponsorship. Um, and I don't just mean
with this, you know, you have an exec
that sends an email and then signs off
on it. No, we actually had our senior
executive leadership team actively
advocating for the use of the tool. They
were sharing at uh town halls, at uh
meetings they were having with their
teams through our existing channels as
well. how they were actually leveraging
the tool, interesting things that they
found out while leveraging the tool,
things that they found helpful in their
learning journey as a way to sort of
build trust, confidence, and encourage
others to also start to take a look at
what's possible with leveraging the
tool. So that active executive
sponsorship, it's not enough to just
have someone who is saying, "Yep, I'll
oversee the project." You need someone
who's actually going to get their hands
dirty, test the tool, and and actively
advocate for it. The second piece is
online of business tailoring. So we knew
that just an enterprisewide, you know,
broad-based messaging was not going to
be enough. We have a very diverse
ecosystem here at CIBC. And like I said,
what a project manager needs is not
necessarily what a frontline employee or
an executive leader is going to be
looking for either. So to complement the
generic me uh messaging which we know
can underperform every line of business
was provided with communication material
and we work directly with those folks
not only to tailor the messaging but to
ensure that we were leveraging the right
channels and the right messengers to
cascade that effectively. So for
example, I can say we embedded some of
that messaging in the huddle material
that went into the banking centers and
for you know some of our other groups
they have monthly newsletters that they
leverage and so we ensured that that
messaging was going through there but
that sort of tailored approach I think
is the key differentiator to ensuring
that this lands um because that generic
messaging doesn't really speak to anyone
and people want to see themselves in the
story and if they can't envision
themselves in the story then they aren't
that interested in changing their ways
of working. The third piece here is on
accessible learning content. And so, you
know, I know we've all been in
situations where we've taken e-learnings
and it's felt overwhelming. Um,
especially thinking about the
apprehension associated with leveraging
AI. We wanted to ensure the learning
content that we built was accessible and
bite-sized and digestible. So, we're
very intentional in how it was created.
Uh, we have bite-sized demo videos. Um,
we also ran AMA sessions really just to
create a low pressure environment so
that folks could access information on
demand and quickly orient themselves
without having to feel like they needed
to become an expert overnight. Um, and
we found very positive results and
feedback to that.
And the fourth piece here is on our
global change network. I would argue
this is probably the most important
lever that uh led to the success of our
rollout. So we currently have uh a
global change champion network of over
1,000 profession proficient users of Kai
across our organization and they
actually sit in each of our lines of
business. And so prior to launch,
engaging with these folks, um we were
able to not only provide them with
messaging, but they could cascade their
teams, but they actually acted almost
like agents on the ground who could tell
us what they were hearing, where those
pain points were sitting. And then we
could actually take a little bit more of
a tailored approach to go and see like
here are some of the sort of heated
areas that we can go in and and provide
some support to and really understand
what the root cause is around that lack
of adoption. Um so that really was a key
differentiator for us. So with those
sort of conditions in place around um
you know launching this tool then I can
maybe
uh go into the next piece here which is
once it's launched how do you actually
keep adoption alive? Um one of the
biggest pieces I'll call out is leader
enablement. So, no one wants to hear
from the project team, unfortunately.
Um, but they do want to hear from
someone that they trust and who is close
to them. And so, if you can equip your
managers and your people leaders with
messaging and resources that they can
then cascade down to their teams, you're
in a much better place to build that
trust and confidence than you are if
it's coming from a stranger who's
working on a strange initiative that no
one's heard about. Um so I would say
that managerled messaging beats top down
any day. And then of course we were
actively measuring um the success of
this throughout the rollout as well. So
we don't just track login and usage,
we're actually tracking fluency to
understand how folks are progressing
with their proficiency of using the
tool. We also used our chain champion
network again to create those feedback
loops where we're actually hearing the
feedback live on the ground where
they're saying, "Hey, this feature we
wish it could do XYZ. that's why we're
not using it. We could go and talk to
the team, see what's possible,
understand if we could, you know, think
about some workarounds. Or there's some
groups who were saying like, we don't
really understand how to use this tool
and it feels overwhelming. Okay, we can
come in and, you know, provide you with
a little bit more of white glove service
with an AMA session or providing you
with a a personalized walkthrough
leveraging use cases that are relevant
to your team. Um, and so that really
helped us enable real- time course
correction. So, we kind of nip in the
butt any sort of resistance as we're
moving through it. And then the the
seventh piece here is on monthly partner
briefings. Um so what I'll say is that
as a project team we understand like
there is only so many places we can be
at one time. And so the best way that we
can equip our business to continue to
funnel adoption forward is to equip them
with information and briefings that they
can then cascade to their teams. And so
on a monthly basis, we connect in with
our communication, business
effectiveness training partners across
each of our lines of business because we
know they understand that business
better than we do. But we can give them
the information that they can then
tailor, cascade, you know, uh, leverage
to then cascade down in the right
channels and to the right people. And
the final piece here, which I think is
often overlooked, is around
psychological safety. So we ran many ask
me anything sessions. Um, and this is
really because people need a space where
they feel like it's okay to ask
questions and get a walk through and and
receive some really um I want to say
tailored support. And sometimes it can
feel a little bit intimidating to ask
for that, especially if your team
members around you are all adopting this
very quickly and using terminology that
you don't necessarily understand. And so
providing sort of a space where they're
able to um uh ask those questions and
attend a bit of an open forum we found
to be very key to adoption driver. And
I'll say these sessions continue to book
out every single week where we are it's
a full house. So that just goes to show
that that space is really important for
our team members to continue to evolve
in their AI fluency and their overall
journey.

think one thing that I wanted to call
out was just around um some of our
lessons learned. So maybe what we didn't
expect. Um I think one of the things

anxious population and they will get

pivotal part of that. Um, and what I
have there on the bottom is, you know,
you have your eager early adopters and
your anxious resistors, but where

a winning adoption strategy.
